rows.description: A teenager writes a slogan for a campaign, a caption for a photo or a script for a skit. Short forms compress attitude and identity, and can be read differently by different audiences.

rows.description: A teenager may find that a joking message reads as rude or a serious one as a joke, since face and voice are missing. Adding an emoji, a clarifying line or a call can avoid conflict.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager uses reaction buttons, hearts and thumbs-up to show quick support or agreement. These are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read as rejection.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
rows.description: A teenager replies with a meme or GIF to convey humour, mood or belonging. Context and audience shape meaning, and an in-joke may confuse or hurt outsiders.

rows.description: A teenager chooses photos, filters and captions to present a self to peers. Posts are curated, so they do not show the full picture of someone's life, and personal images should be shared only with consent and care.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager reads "okay." as cold, "OKAY!!!" as shouting or excitement, and "sooooo" as emphasis or playfulness. Norms differ by group, age and platform, so such cues suggest but do not prove a mood.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Drama and mime as emotional language [Expressing]
rows.description: A teenager uses acting, mime or improvisation to portray feelings that are hard to say aloud, such as grief or anger. Role work lets emotion be explored at a safe distance, but it is not a confession of real events.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: grief, anger, trust

rows.subtype: Playlists and dance trends as mood signals [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager shares a sad song or a viral dance video online, which may mean mood, humour, belonging or mere fashion. A brief kind check-in works better than assuming distress from one post.

rows.description: A teenager writes verses or slam poetry about identity, injustice, love or loneliness. Lyrics use persona and exaggeration, so a listener should ask the writer before assuming the words describe their real plans.
